Every engine story feature is exercised: linear narration, character dialogue, choice hubs with voiceKeywords + completionFlag elimination, combat triggers (triggerBattleEncounterId + nextNodeId), scene changes (changeSceneId), hub auto-redirect when all flags are set (hubCompletion), companion reclass (joinWhenFlag on the reclassified Todd), the grievance arcs, the CC-regional secret protocol, a victory chain, and the engine-convention 'game_completed' flag that ends the playthrough at the close of Act Six. All names, titles, and policies are fictional (Content Neutrality: see AGENTS.md).

nodes.text: 3:47 in the morning, Provo. A Wally's World megamart sits in the dark like a poured slab of concrete waiting to be alive. Behind the building, a trailer is backed up to the bay door, forty-eight feet of freight, and it is not going to unload itself. Speak aloud to advance, or say 'Options' at any time.
The clock says I should be asleep. The register says otherwise. Somebody's got to pull this line, and today that somebody is me.
The building hums. Half a dozen lawn chairs and a ten-year-old coffee maker sit in the break pit like a monument. Speak a choice aloud, or tap it.

choices.text: Learn the freight line before you touch it.
Meet the overnight crew in the break pit.
Brew the ancient coffee before anyone needs it.
Throw the bay door open and run the unload.
Head up to the sales floor to see what the day holds.

nodes.text: The line has a rhythm: case, scan, slot, move on. Step off the rhythm and the boxes stack up behind you until they're taller than you are. The line is honest. The line does not care who you are.
The overnight crew is four bodies in lawn chairs and one in a trucker hat. They don't look up much. One of them makes room for you on the cooler. That's the welcome. Hold on to it.
You find the old grounds, the cracked carafe, and the water that tastes like the back of the store. You brew it anyway. By the time the crew smells it, you're already somebody.
The bay door rattles up and the freight is right there, wall to wall. The fluorescents start their whine. Say 'Enemies' anytime to scan the field — and remember, speak sharp and it lands harder.
Pallet by pallet, the wall comes down. My back is loud about it, but the trailer is empty before the sun comes up.
You ride the pallet jack up to the sales floor and the doors slide apart into a hundred thousand square feet of house, garden, food, and florescent sky.

The morning walkie crackles. The store manager's voice — Mattie-T, they call him, because his last name is one letter and nobody says the rest — calls for the overnight supervisor. There is no supervisor.

The title lands before the raise does: Freight Supervisor. It means I'm still hauling freight, and now I'm the one who explains why the freight is late. Corners of the store I didn't know existed are suddenly mine.
The floor stretches out, waiting. What do you do with your new little square of the machine?

choices.text: Take the overnight crews to the floor and lead the morning.
Rebuild the stocking process from the label sheets up.
Hold the floor through the front-end storm.
Walk up to the front end and see the machine's mouth.

nodes.text: I tell the overnight crew the only thing I believe: nobody gets left to ride the wave alone. A body goes down, the line stops for a body. We move freight, and we move it together.
You rebuild the process from the label sheets up: zones, flow, the four big aisles running like arteries. The numbers climb. The walkie goes quiet. Somebody upstairs notices.
The hour-occupancy gauge is deep in the red and the pages start firing. Front-end storm. Everybody on the floor.
Customers leave with their carts and their receipts. The gauge drips back down to green. I stand in the middle of the floor, breathing like it's the first time.
You head for the front of the building, where the registers face the parking lot and the machine shows its face to the public.

The front end is the machine's mouth. Every register is a slot in a wall. And at the back of it, behind the service desk, Jodie waves you over — your old supervisor manager from the freight days, the one who watched you climb, now running area HR out of Colorado, a manila folder already open in his hands.

I'd watched the layoffs roll through by then. The duffle-bag-of-thousand-cuts kind. I make a promise nobody can hear: if I run a crew, the machine eats numbers, not bodies. I don't know yet how much that promise will cost.

Todd. Sit down for a second. There's a slot opening up — assistant manager track, shop manager slot, the management ladder. It's in Colorado. Lamar. It's not the real thing yet — it's the foot in the door that leads to the real thing. If you take it, you're not an hourly anymore. You're in the machine, on purpose, with a key.
The folder is open on the desk. The truck that could take you to Colorado is parked out front. What do you need to know first?

choices.text: Ask Jodie what the slot really is.
Watch the front end work one more time.
Walk to the manager's office to give the answer.

nodes.text: The slot is real. The pay is real. The hours are real, twice as many as you'd expect, and the first of them is on a store that is on fire, figuratively. Mattie-T knows you're leaving. That's the only part that worries me.

You watch the front end run for ten minutes. It runs. Nobody stops to breathe. The refugees of the last round of cuts are already being retrained to cut the next round. The machine doesn't blink. The machine loves everyone equally.
The manager's office is at the end of the hall, behind the wall of laminated posters. The door is open. The computer is already on.

Mattie-T is behind the desk, smiling the way management smiles. The email is already sent — one short paragraph to Cap'n Skagg, the Colorado area manager, typed after your promotion and before a single position had been assigned. The gist, in his opinion: you weren't ready. Not for a real one.

There it is — the whole equation. The slot Jodie offered didn't fall from the sky; it fell off Cap'n Skagg's desk, and it fell because of an opinion Mattie-T typed out and already sent. I tell him, respectfully, over the quiet: he's wrong about me, and I'll prove it. He doesn't take it back. He can't. The office goes quiet. Somewhere, the building leans on the wall.

The office contracts. The clock on the wall ticks once, and everything Todd has built this act comes at him at once: the email, the squeeze, the whole machine. Speak sharp — say it loud, say it clear.

The email stays sent. That's the rule of the machine — opinions are already out there, writing your story for you. I look at him across the desk, and I don't hate him. The machine doesn't need me to hate him. It needs me to prove him wrong.

Todd. I read that email, and I've known you long enough to know better. Listen — this slot is a foot in the door. One position, out in Lamar. You do the work, and they move you somewhere real after. That's how the ladder works. I vouched for you. Make me right.

By midnight the box truck is packed. Jodie's folder is on the passenger seat, and the keys to the Colorado slot hang off the visor. Todd's behind the wheel, grinning at the old building, already planning the first day. He thinks he knows the worst of what happened there. He doesn't. The gas pump in the lavender light hums like the whole state is holding its breath.

End of Act One. Todd is pointed east on I-70, one state line away from a brand-new store, a brand-new boss, and the slow realization that the machine you left runs on the people you're about to become. He's excited, and he hasn't got a clue how deep that little email ran. Colorado. Lamar. The squeeze is just getting started.

Lamar, Colorado. A tiny dot on the map that somehow gets all the traffic nobody else wants — cross-country semi-trucks, travelers with blown transmissions, local ranchers pulling up in something a decade past its warranty. The service shop is six bays under a sagging canopy, and it smells like fresh motor oil, burning rubber, and winter cold blowing off the high plains.

I'm not an unloader anymore. The title on the folder says Shop Manager — salaried, six bays, oil changes and tire installations and all the hours those papers said they'd be. I walk the line between the lifts and I already feel it: behind the wheel of a place that's mine to run, for better or worse.

You'll do fine out here, sugar. Miss Trudy — the store manager, for a little while longer. They keep telling me to tighten up, but I been running this place on people first and it's held together just fine. You take care of the folks in these bays and they'll take care of you. Most of management never learns that.
The service shop hums around you — lifts, tire machines, air guns, and the permanent smell of grease. The honeymoon window is open. What do you do first?

choices.text: Streamline the bays: safety, parts inventory, and workflow.
Meet the techs and build the crew into a team.
Show Cap'n Skagg around before he leaves the store.
Throw the bays open and run the Friday oil rush.
Close out the year and see where the numbers landed.

nodes.text: You rebuild the bay from the floor up: torque specs on the wall where every tech can see them, parts bins tagged and counted twice a week, the tire machine routed with the line. The work is tangible — tires, oil, batteries — and it responds to attention the way the backroom never quite did.

Four techs and a lube kid who flinches when anyone raises a voice. I run the line with them for a week before I say a word about policy. Somewhere in there it stops being their shop and starts being ours. That's the only kind of crew I know how to run.

Cap'n Skagg. The man who assigns these slots — which means I'm the one who read what Mattie-T sent about you before you ever got here. 'Not ready,' he said. You've been in this shop one week and the bays run like a string of lights.
I tell you what, kid — I'm glad I looked for myself. I train my managers like I'm betting on them, and I just saw what I needed to see.

Friday, 3 PM. Six bays, a line of pickups around the block, and every one of them convinced theirs is the one that has to be done before dark. The rush is a living thing and it wants to own your floor.
By closing, every ticket is turned. The lube kid is standing taller. I'm covered in grease and grinning like I won something, which — for once — maybe I did.

The year closes itself out on the dashboard: top of the company on shrink metrics, service revenue climbing every single month, and a customer satisfaction number that sits at a perfect ten-point-oh for the whole calendar year. It is the best year the service shop has ever seen — and Todd built it with his own crew, his own processes, his own hands.

And then the machine does what the machine does. Miss Trudy — who kept the store humane, who trusted her people, who got results without cruelty — is handed her 'early retirement' in a meeting that lasts nine minutes. It wasn't her choice. It's never their choice. The store's heart is quietly removed and the air goes cold waiting for whoever they send next.

Don't you go gettin' angry for me, sugar. I been in this building forty years and I knew the number was coming. They'll send somebody to tighten the whole place up — that's what they always do. You keep running that shop the way you run it. You were the best thing that happened to these bays, and I'm proud I got to watch it.

They send Jury. She arrives on a Monday with a binder, a trim smile, and a single sentence she says to every department head before she's unpacked her office: she doesn't care about your results as long as nothing reaches the region.
Nothing bounces upward to the region. That is your only job, and it is the whole job. I don't care about your bay metrics as long as it's quiet. Keep it quiet.
The friendly store is gone. The watchful eye is on everything — cameras, check-ins, the walkie chirping with suspicion. How do you hold your crew together under the new regime?

choices.text: Learn the pattern of the watchful eye.
Shield the bay crew from the tightening grip.
Stand against the purge audit on the store floor.
Ask Cap'n Skagg what this purge means for the area.
Move on and see what the new regime demands next.

nodes.text: You learn the pattern quickly: Jury doesn't care about results, only that nothing surfaces. The eye blinks only when someone reaches for the door that leads upward. So you learn the geometry of the blind spots — for no dark reason. So your people can breathe in them.

The bays are my line. If Jury wants a scalp every quarter, she can have the papers — but not the people. I keep the techs on the lift schedule, on their breaks, on their feet. The watch can see everything except what I decide it can't.

The purge audit moves through the building like weather: the retirement memo, Jury's gaze, and the old hum of the fluorescents pressing in from every ceiling. This one comes at the department all at once.

The audit passes without a single name of mine on the paper. The eye blinks, repositioned. I chalk it up and keep my head down, but I've started to notice: the machine never needed Miss Trudy's heart to run — it just needed a place to hold it where it couldn't get in the way.

Trudy was the best store manager I had in this area and the company retired her like a used tire. Don't mistake that for accident, kid — that was the machine pruning what doesn't fit. You're fitting, that's why you're still here. Keep fitting. I'm not allowed to say more than that.

Home, after a long one. Adriana is at the table with a stack of papers and a look you know better than to walk past. She's applied — internally, to the open Shop Manager position up in the next town over. The kind of step up that two incomes were finally going to let the family take.

The wall between the family and a better life is not a wall at all — it's a process. A week of forms, a polite interview in an area office, and one sentence spoken to Adriana that the paperwork will never contain the same way she'll hear it forever.

I went to the interview — went in with the resume, the experience, the hours, everything they said they wanted. The interviewer was very polite about it. They wanted a man for the job. That's what they said. They didn't even try to hide it, Todd. They just... wanted a man.

I sit there at the kitchen table and I can feel the heat go all the way down into my boots. This is the machine, and I know what the machine does with a grievance. But Adriana is looking at me, and the word is on the record, and some doors you open anyway even when you know the answer.
The grievance paperwork sits on the kitchen table — the formal grievance to the area level, typed, signed, witnessed by no one but the two of you. What's the first move?

choices.text: Write down everything said in the interview, word for word.
Call Jodie in Area HR and ask how the process works.
Slip the grievance into the machine and let it grind.
Wait out the week and hear what they decide.

nodes.text: You write it down the way she said it, plain and unembellished: the resume, the interview, and the sentence — they wanted a man for the job — written in a room, on a record, in front of nobody but them. It is the cleanest truth you have ever typed into a corporate form.

Todd. I'm not supposed to tell you this. The process is a week long, the investigator talks to the people who said it, and they will deny it, and the form will come back and say exactly one word. I've seen a hundred of these. I'll flag it, because I know you both — but the machine isn't built for this one to come back your way.

The grievance is submitted, and for a week the machinery grinds: the file, the man they wanted, the polite denials wearing the shape of review panels. The grievance was never a door — but you stand in front of it anyway, because someone has to.

The machinery grinds and grinds and produces nothing but the same noise. I stand there in the hallway of the area office with the folder in my hand, and I already know what the stamp is going to say before they say it.

Unsubstantiated. The investigator spoke to the very managers who uttered it, accepted their denial at face value, and closed the file. No appeal letter is acknowledged. No transcript is kept. The door closes with the same soft click the machine gives every door it never opened.

The annual associate Christmas party arrives like a duty: a rented community hall, fluorescent glare, bad catering, and everyone pretending the store is one big family while the store watches from the ceiling like it always does.

The hall is loud and overlit. The punch is mostly ginger ale. And across the room, Jury is doing what Jury does — making her presence known, drink in hand, looking for the person in the room she can afford to be cruel to. That person, tonight, has your name on it.

She walks right up to you, in front of witnesses, and with casual malice in her voice she calls you the word — twice. Not a slip. Deliberate. The room goes a half-beat quiet. Somewhere a paper cup hits the floor. And Todd stands there with the whole party looking at him.

I don't swing. I don't shout. I feel it land and I hold it, because I know — I know with my whole body — that the second grievance is already signing itself in my pocket. The party goes back to its noise. I go to the men's room and write the date on my palm.

The second grievance is filed that same night — the complaint against a store manager who degraded an associate in front of witnesses. The machine now has twice the paperwork and exactly the same answer. What do you do while it grinds?

choices.text: Swallow it in front of the crew so the party stays whole.
Tell Adriana what happened as soon as you're both home.
Face Jury in the glare of the hall, in front of everyone.
Wait out the grind and hear the machine's answer.

nodes.text: You hold the room together — working the punch line, laughing at the right moments, making sure not one tech goes home with the look on their face that says the manager's cruelty is contagious. The party survives. You file the report on the drive home, one hand on the wheel.

You tell me and I can see it — the way it sits in you, the way you're already doing the math on whether filing it is worth it. Todd. It is worth it. Even if they stamp it again. Even if they stamp it forever. You are worth it. And we are not staying anywhere that treats either of us like this.

The confrontation comes at you out of the fluorescent glare — jury's malice, the file that never closes, and the whole weight of the machine standing between you and the door. In front of everyone, it all comes at once.

I take it all and I hold the line until the room breathes again. She's already walked away, laughing like it never happened. That's the part you learn to hate worst — not the cruelty, but how weightless it is to them.

Unsubstantiated. Again. The investigator — the same one — spoke to the very person who said it, who denied it, and the file closed with the same stamp, the same click. And there, under the fluorescent light of the area office,

Todd finally understands the foundational truth of the retail machine: truth, ethics, and human dignity do not exist inside this system. Only liability exists. And if an admission creates liability, the corporate apparatus will aggressively lie to protect itself.

Weeks pass. The store keeps eating its people and the town keeps pretending it doesn't. And then, one ordinary morning in the bays, the pain arrives — a burning, agonizing line of fire across your forehead. Shingles Outbreak Number One. The body keeps the score, and it has been scoring for a long, long time.
It starts on my forehead — a line of fire drawn across the skin, hot as a belt of coals. The doctor uses the word shingles and it lands like a sentence.

The body doesn't care about CSAT scores or shrink metrics — it kept its own ledger, and this is the balance. I stand in the bays looking at the lifts and I know, before I say anything to anyone, that we're leaving.

We talk about it the way we've talked about every real thing — sitting at the table, honest, no performance. South Carolina. The East Coast, the long-held dream. And we pay for it out of our own pocket, every cent, because a relocation benefit contract around our necks is how the machine keeps you — and we are done letting it keep us. We leave on our own terms, with nothing owed and nothing weighing us down.

The truck fills up over two weeks: box after box, the house shrinking into the driveway. But before the last box goes in, Cap'n Skagg pulls up to the curb — the area manager, on his own time, doing the one thing the machine never authorized.

choices.text: Fight through the nerve fire to finish the load.
Say goodbye to Cap'n Skagg by the packed truck.
Load the last box and point the truck east.

nodes.text: The boxes are half in and the pain is a living thing across your forehead — the first outbreak, the body's own scorecard, demanding you stop. You fight it the way you've fought every other thing in your life: one box at a time, through the fire, until the truck is full.
The last box goes in and the pain is still there — it will be there for weeks — but I load every single one anyway. The body can keep score all it wants. It doesn't get to keep us.

I read both files, kid. I read what they stamped on 'em. And I want you to know — I didn't come here as Area Manager. I came here as a man who watched you run that shop like it mattered, who saw the machine take a good woman off the floor and a better one at your kitchen table. You're gonna build something real, out there where a person can breathe. And if you ever run a shop in my area again, I'll be first in line to bet on you.

The truck is packed, the apartment is empty, and Lamar is in the mirror. Todd and Adriana leave Colorado the same way they came into it — together, out of pocket, pointed east with the scar of the first outbreak burning across Todd's forehead like a receipt for everything the machine took and everything they refused to give it. Georgia first, then the state line, then a service shop in South Carolina that doesn't know them yet. End of Act Two — the borderlands ahead.

South of the Georgia state line, the sun comes up over a scrub-pine horizon and the traffic crawls toward the border. A rented house sits dark behind you, coffee still warm in the cup, Adriana asleep in a bed that smells like cardboard and fresh paint.
Somewhere across the Savannah River, a Wally's World service shop is waiting to learn what you do to a place that has been left to run on its own for too long.
The drive is the boundary — a hundred and twelve miles between who I am and what I do. Home is the pine woods and the porch light. Work is the concrete and the grease.

I pass the welcome sign at the state line and the radio swaps itself to a station I don't know, and I tell myself the same thing I told Provo and Lamar: this time, I'll keep the promise. The scar under my hat brim doesn't answer.

The shop is six bays under a roof that hasn't been repainted since the previous decade. Toolboxes missing wheels, a wall of work orders nobody has touched, parts stacked in unlabeled bins like a hoard. The crew is a mixed bag — a couple of seasoned techs who keep their eyes down, and three green apprentices who look at the lifts like the lifts might bite. Deferred maintenance, every square inch of it. The whole place has been waiting for someone to care — or for someone to sign the wrong thing.

The neglected shop hums around you — compressors, tire machines, and the quiet weight of years of nobody running the line. The honeymoon window is open here too, same as everywhere. What do you do first?

choices.text: Learn the true state of the bays before you touch anything.
Meet the techs and apprentices over the shop's sad coffee.
Drive home across the state line and end the day the right way.
Take the first work order and fight the neglect head-on.
Close out the week and learn how this store is actually run.

nodes.text: You do a slow, honest walk of the bay floor: torque wrenches with dead calibration stickers, a lift that groans when it should be silent, brake gauges nobody remembers recalibrating. In one bin you find a stack of lug

nuts that came off a wheel because somebody didn't tighten them to spec. You tag every defect on a clipboard. Nobody stops you. That's the first bad sign — in a healthy shop, somebody would have argued.
The seasoned techs give you the once-over and go back to their tickets — they've seen managers come and go, and they have one rule: show them you can turn a wrench and they'll talk.

The apprentices are different. They watch you like you might be the person who finally explains the job instead of just screaming about it. You make a pot of coffee. It's terrible. It's the best coffee you've made anywhere.

The porch light is on across the state line, and I'm still awake because I wanted to hear how it went. Don't give me the brave version. Give me the real one — that shop has been left to rot, you can smell it on

yourself, and you think you can fix it the way you fixed Lamar. Maybe you can. But Todd — watch your back there. A place that's been neglected this long has reasons it stayed that way, and they're not always yours to carry.

Your first ticket drops six minutes after the bays open — brakes, four wheels, and a clock that's already running. The neglect is a living thing in the room with you: the groaning lift, the dead gauges, the whole building daring you to care. Say 'Enemies' anytime to size up the fight. Speak sharp — it lands harder.

By closing, the ticket is turned and the apprentice who watched me torque every lug nut by hand asked why. Because they're the last thing between a family and a ditch, that's why. The shop didn't lower its walls today, but it looked at me different — like the man who knew what the job was.

The week closes. The bays run straighter, the parts bins gain labels, and for a handful of days it almost feels like the plan is working. Then the walkies crackle all at once: the quarterly leadership tour is coming, and this store's version of 'leadership' is about to show you exactly where you stand in it.

The executive pack descends on the building like weather: six people in pressed shirts and polished shoes, flanked by the area manager and the region's compliance voice. The whole store knows before they've parked — the tours are the one day the building holds its breath and hopes nobody points at a dent.

The rules are rigid and total: only the Store Manager walks with the visitors. Every junior salaried manager — every department head, every shop manager, every one of the people who actually run the building — is told to stay on the floor and keep the store looking alive. You stand at the edge of the sales floor and watch the glass doors close on the tour before a single question is asked.

There she is — the Store Manager, walking the pack with a smile I've already learned to read. Azalia. Kind to everyone, quick with a name and a birthday, and right now she's nodding at whatever the compliance voice is saying about the shop.
I'm locked out of the room where my own department is being decided. The lesson from Colorado was that the machine lies to protect itself. Here the machine doesn't even bother to let you in the room.

The edict comes down before the visitors' cars leave the lot: turn times cut across the service shop, sign-off streamlined, every ticket on a clock. Nobody on the floor was consulted. Nobody on the floor was asked if the bays could physically do it. The toolboxes that lost their wheels aren't going to grow them back because a visitor said 'tighten it up.'

The tour is gone and the edict is running through the building like a current. The other locked-out managers are on the floor with you, doing the math on what just got sold out from under them. What do you do with the rest of this day?

choices.text: Watch the rest of the walkthrough's shadow land on the floor.
Scope the edict with the other locked-out managers.
Endure the edict as it hits the bay floor all at once.
Move on and learn what the kind store manager actually does with power.

nodes.text: You watch it happen in real time: the visitors' compliments get translated into new screens and new penalties, the parts of the store that shone that morning get flagged for audits they can't possibly pass, and a lube kid who waved at the wrong moment gets pulled off the floor. The tour didn't take a single question from the people who run the building. It took everything it wanted.

The other managers gather in the hallway and do the arithmetic out loud. The turn-time edict is impossible as written — bodies short, bay count fixed, parts bins still unlabeled. Every one of them has watched an impossible number get handed down before. Only one of them mentions going up the chain, and they all laugh at him. That's not the kind of thing you laugh about.

The edict slams into the bays at once — the new clock over every ticket, the compliance voice in every ear, the whole building leaning on the line to make an impossible number real. It's not a memo. It's a gauntlet, and it's already running.

The floor holds. Turn times stay human, and under the new clocks the bays do what they do — the work gets done, the tickets turn, nobody gets hurt. But I come out of it with the same feeling I had in Lamar: the machine doesn't care how hard we hold the line. It only cares what it can pile on top of the line next.

The tour becomes the creak in the building's floor — the sound you hear every morning and learn to live with. And the kind store manager, the one everyone says is wonderful, is about to show you what 'wonderful' costs when the room needs something harder than a smile.

Azalia is a contradiction you can't quite file. She's the store manager and your boss, and she remembers your wife's name after one conversation. She sends a card when the shop fixes your hot water heater, and when an apprentice's grandmother passes she cries a little and tells the kid to take the week — no questions, no forms. The shop is yours to run: you own the bays, the tickets, and the discipline. Walk the floor with her and the store feels almost humane. Then watch what happens the first time you hold somebody accountable.

Todd. I heard what you did with the bays — the torque board, the labels, the way the apprentices are standing taller. That's wonderful, that's exactly what this shop needed. I mean that — and I mean it as your store manager.

The shop is your shop; I trust you with it down to the last wrench. Listen, if you ever need anything — anything for your family, for your crew, for yourself — my door is open. I know I don't say it enough, but the people in this building are the reason I stay in this job.

Accountability is your job, and you do it: the corner-cutting tech — the one whose tickets come back with missing steps, who logs work he never did — gets written up in ink. Missing steps, logged hours, tickets that could cost somebody money or worse. You sign it, you date it, you hand him the copy, and for one night the shop has a consequence in it.

Then Azalia finds out. Day two, the write-up is gone from the file, your signature circled in the margin like a question. She took the tech aside herself — gently, warmly — and everything you put in writing was un-written. Not denied, not disputed: unmade. The kindness absorbs accountability like a sponge, and the problem stays exactly where it was.

Enforcing cost you more than the failure itself: every consequence you draw gets unmade before the ink dries, and every tech in the bays knows it. You care, and caring in this building makes you the bad guy — the one who keeps writing fair paperwork that the store manager kindly disappears. What do you do with what you just learned?

choices.text: Give Azalia one more chance to be the good version of herself.
Hold the failing tech accountable yourself, carefully.
Push against the paralysis directly while it still has a cost.
Move on — the corner-cutting is only going to get worse from here.

nodes.text: I'm glad you came back to me, Todd. I know how hard your people work, and how little thanks they get — I'd take a bullet for this crew, honestly I would. But that write-up, love — do you really need it? That boy has a grandmother he just buried and two kids at home.

I read every line, and I know you wrote it fair; that's why I like you. But I can't live with the smell of somebody's spirit breaking over a ticket. So let me handle him. Gently. I'm his store manager, I'll set him straight in my way — you'll see. You have the best heart in this building, Todd. Let me be the soft part. Please.

I do what no one else in this building will: I sit the tech down in the bay and I say it plainly — the corners stop here, the work gets verified, or the next conversation is with someone who can actually sign a termination. He looks at me like I've grown a second head. Not because I'm wrong.

Because in this store, nobody says the quiet part aloud anymore — the store manager hears every write-up, reads it twice, and makes it disappear before anybody has to feel it. I know the paper's fate the moment I sign it. I sign it anyway. My name on a fair document is the last honest thing in that building.

The paralysis is a living pressure in the room — the smile that unmakes every consequence, the warmth that never weighs, the whole building learning that nothing you put in writing will ever stick. It wants to teach you the same lesson. Say 'Enemies' and ready yourself — this one smiles while it grinds.

The line holds — the corners stop, the tech steps back from the edge, and for now, in my bays, the work is real again. But I walk back to the office with the truth sitting heavy in me: I didn't win against the paralysis.
I won a round against one man's carelessness. The smile at the front of the store is still there, and as soon as I put this in writing it will unmake it — the way it unmakes everything I sign.

The weeks pass and the quiet part gets louder. Under the turn-time clocks, with no consequence anywhere in the building, the corner-cutting stops being a whisper and starts being a habit. Somewhere in the bays, somebody is about to learn what a habit like that costs. And the machine is already looking for who to blame.

The signs are all there if you know how to read them: a tech who stops using the torque wrench because the clock is faster without it, brake pads that get slapped in without a look at the rotors, an apprentice fussed and rushed because the edict counts tickets, not safety. You've flagged every one of them. The file on your desk is the only consequence in the building — and it's yours.

I draw the line where the line has always been: I will not sign off on work I can't verify. A wheel is torque-checked or it doesn't leave the bay. A brake job gets the caliper measured or it gets redone. Azalia pulls me aside — gently, warmly — and says the visitors need the numbers, and the numbers need the rush, and doesn't that sound reasonable? She has unmade two of my write-ups this month; I know the soft voice by now. I tell her no, it sounds like a lawsuit with my name on it. That's the whole conversation.

Three days later it happens. A sedan comes off the lift and loses a wheel in the back lot — not at speed, not on the road, but it comes off, and the wheel rolls under a parked truck and stops. Nobody is hurt. The whole building knows.

And within the hour, the store is already working the story: the lug nuts were loose before the bay, the tech is reliable, the car was fine until the lot, and the only person who kept saying the shop was unsafe was the shop manager who 'slows everything down.' The fall guy is being pre-fitted before the tire is back on.

The near-miss is being buried in real time — the report rewritten, the witnesses reminded what they didn't see, the blame sliding toward the one manager who refused to sign. You've been here before, twice. But you learned something in Colorado that this store doesn't know you know. What's the move?

Use the secret protocol: run the grievance straight past the store — CC regional.

nodes.text: I write it the way it happened — the loose wheel, the missing torque spec, the two weeks of flagged corners, the file that was the only consequence in the building. I sign my name and I date it and I write 'Signed under protest' where they asked me to approve the final report. They can bury a report. They can't delete the copy that's already in my hand.

The protocol from Colorado, the one hard lesson that pays: don't feed the grievance to the store, don't feed it to the area desk where it will be stamped and closed. You skip the lower tiers entirely and take the complaint straight

to regional — one email, one CC line that runs past every smiling gatekeeper in the building. It's the only lever you already know is real. The machine flinches when you touch it. That's not a good sign for them.

The blame comes for you at the end of the week: the rewritten report, the visit to the area office, the smile asking if you'd like to reconsider your version of events. It's the same gauntlet as the brick wall in Colorado — except this time the wheel in the lot was real, and you have the file. Hold the line.

They can't make my report say what it doesn't say. They can't make my signature appear where it isn't. I walk out of the area office with the file still in my hand and the whole weight of the store telling me I just ended my own time here. Maybe I did. But I didn't end it lying.

Now the real fight — the one the store never expected you to pick. The regional desk sits three hundred miles away behind phones and calendars, built to absorb complaints until they fossilize. But you didn't call the desk. You ran the line past the people above it, and the desk knows the difference. Fight the machine from the outside of the machine, where the smile has no power.

The complaint moves. Not fast, not fairly, but it moves — the way the brick wall in Colorado never once moved. I read the response twice. Somewhere a stranger with a title I'll never meet has actually read my file. It's the first time in three years the machine has blinked when I pushed. It's not justice. It's a crack. A crack is a start.

Two weeks later the verdict lands, and it is the strangest thing the store has ever seen: regional actually acts. An inspector walks the shop floor unannounced, the loose-wheel report is pulled and reopened, and the corner-cutter is quietly moved to a position with no torque wrench and no clock.

It's not punishment. It's not even discipline. It's liability insurance — regional decided the pattern was cheaper to fix than to bury. For one small week, the machine moved because someone stood on the outside of it and pushed.

And that's when I know we're leaving. Not because regional acted — because of what it took. The store celebrated the fix like the fix was its own idea. Azalia smiled at me, warm as ever, like none of it happened. The building had a near-miss on its conscience and the only real consequence was a transfer nobody cares about and a shop manager the whole store now resents. This place will eat someone else the way it tried to eat me. I stand in the bays, and the scar on my forehead already knows what comes next.

Weeks later, on an ordinary morning at the bays, the pain returns — the familiar, burning line of fire across your forehead, drawn in the same place as the first one, like the body keeps perfect records of every store in every state. Shingles Outbreak Number Two. The body has been scoring all along, and the second entry is written where everyone can see it.

Second time, I know it before the doctor says it. I stand in the mirror in the shop's back room and look at the line of fire above my eyebrow, and I think about what my body is trying to tell me: ethical compromise and systemic neglect burn the nervous system exactly the way impossible metrics do. I stopped signing the machine's lies. The machine is a lie you still have to live beside. Not for much longer.

I see it on your forehead the second you walk in, and I don't need the word. You've been carrying that shop on your spine since the tour, and now the body has weighed in. So here's what we do — we go back to Colorado.

Pueblo. They've got a stocking overhaul starting, and word is they need managers who actually know how to run a crew. No more borderlands, Todd. No more kind smile over an open wound. We pack the porch, and we go somewhere a person can breathe.

The Georgia porch light burns out the night before the packing starts. The truck rental is booked, Pueblo is a dot on a map three states away, and the machine doesn't know you're leaving yet. Say what needs to be said before the last box goes in.

choices.text: Fight through the second nerve fire to finish the load.
Take Azalia's goodbye by the door while she still has one.
Load the last box and point the truck west.

nodes.text: The second outbreak is a living thing across your forehead — the same fire as the first, hotter for knowing exactly where it came from. The truck is half full and the body is demanding you stop, again, the way it demanded in Lamar. You fight it the way you've fought everything: one box at a time, through the fire, until the load is done.

The last box goes in and the pain is still there — it will be there for weeks, the way it always is — but I load every one of them anyway. The body can keep score all it wants. It doesn't get to keep us. That was true in Lamar and it's true here.

Todd. I'm so sorry to see you go — you really were the best thing that happened to those bays, and I mean that with my whole heart. Colorado, huh? That's where you're from. I hope it's everything the borderlands weren't. We'll miss you. We'll miss your wife too — tell her I still have the card she sent, it's on my desk.

The warmth is seamless, weightless, complete — the same kindness that unmade every consequence you ever drew. She means every word of it. That's the terrible part. The kindness was never a lie; it just could never let anything stick.
Even at the very end, with the truck in the driveway and the file in your coat, the door closes on a woman who truly liked you and would let the next wheel come off exactly the same way.

The truck is packed, the porch light is dark, and the Georgia pines are in the mirror. Todd and Adriana leave the borderlands with the second scar burning across Todd's forehead like a ledger entry — one outbreak per state, one store per price paid.
Ahead: Pueblo, Colorado — the madness, the overhaul, the longest squeeze the machine will ever put on them. They drive west together, owing the machine nothing — for now. End of Act Three.

The driveshaft of the country: I-25 south out of the Front Range, and Pueblo sitting in its bowl of prairie heat and steel-town haze. The store is a slab of concrete and light on the edge of the sprawl — big enough to swallow the borderlands shop whole. The office slot they hired you for says Stocking Manager. The building will tell you what that really means by nine o'clock tonight.

Stocking manager, they said on the phone from the region. Closing manager, it turns out — and not the kind with a crew. I'm the only salaried body in the building from the moment the evening comes until the last light goes out. The org chart shows hourly supervisors under me. I've never met one. They exist somewhere on paper. That's where they stay.

The store at dusk is a zoo being fed one aisle at a time: the registers backing up, the service desk blinking, the parking lot doing whatever the parking lot does. And it's yours — all of it, alone. What do you do with your first close?

choices.text: Walk the building and learn what actually breaks at night.
Meet the closing crew before the sun is gone.
Hold the front end as the queues stack to the doors.
Close the store alone at midnight — every light, every till.
Let the night happen and see what it brings.

nodes.text: You walk it once, slow, before the last daylight goes: the tills, the safe, the emergency exits, the receiving door, the walkie channel that pages a supervisor who is never there. Every system on the closing checklist routes through one person. The manual says four. The building says one — and tonight that one is you.

The closing crew is five bodies in teal and orange: an old cashier who calls everyone hon, two kids folding freight carts, a tired woman on the service desk, and a courtesy clerk whose name you already forgot — because they'll need to be three different people before midnight.
None of them has a supervisor to call. They look at you the way the borderlands apprentices did: like you might be the one who explains the job instead of screaming about it.

Nine o'clock and the queues stack six deep at every open register, the service desk is blinking like a strobe, and the walkie is dead air because there's no one left to page. The swarm of the evening is a living thing and it wants your floor. Say 'Enemies' to size it up — speak sharp and it lands harder.

A man at the front of the line demands to know his number. I tell him the truth: he's number six. There are five ahead of him I haven't saved yet, and I'm running to the service desk to save one of them.
He doesn't believe me. He watches me go — I move, and he stays, and somewhere behind me the queue breathes a little softer for knowing someone's actually running it.

Midnight. The last customer is out, the doors are locked, and what's left is yours: forty thousand square feet of dark, every till to count, every light to kill, every door to check — and the building, empty,
pressing in like it's keeping count of you too. The One-Man Close. It has one rule: don't let it find a corner you missed. Say 'Enemies' — then close it like it's yours, because it is.
I finish the count by one in the morning, lock the safe, and stand in the dark at the front doors looking out at the empty lot. Not a single supervisor. Not a single backup.
Just me and the keys and a building that's already planning tomorrow's crowd. It's the loneliest I've been in retail — and I already care about the crew in that building too much to leave them to it.

A year passes like a bad shift: one close after another, no help hired, no supervisors grown. The nights develop a texture of their own. Somewhere in that first year the building teaches you things no training video ever covered.

A customer goes down in front of the pharmacy — mid-aisle, eyes open, body shaking, the seizure coming on the way they do at the worst possible second. You page the supervisors' channel. Nothing answers. It hasn't answered in eleven months. You're already on the floor with him, one hand under his head, one hand on the phone, the whole store standing at a polite, frozen distance.

By the time the medics get there he's breathing fine and trying to apologize — to me, for the trouble. I tell him don't. I walk him out to the ambulance and I stand in the lot a minute, thinking: one person. Forty thousand feet. No help at all. That's the whole job description.
Some nights the store is a meeting point for people who should not be meeting. Two groups of young men, two colors no one in this building picked, decide the café corner belongs to one of them
— and it ends the way it always does: voices, shoving, a display of glass going down. The security guard they hired is one person, off shift by nine. There's no one to call except you.

I get between them — not brave, just the only option. I walk them out the side doors one group at a time, and I stand in the doorway while they decide whether the parking lot counts. They leave. Nobody got hurt. I locked up and wrote the whole thing in the log like it was a normal Tuesday, because in this building, it was.

A year, Todd. One night shift after another, and every time I ask, they still don't have anyone to help you close. You come home with that walkie dead in your pocket and your eyes doing the count of the tills.
I see the scar starting to pale on your forehead, and I pray it stays pale — but I know what it looked like before, and I know the store you're running is the reason.

Year two begins with a phone call that doesn't come from the store: a regional voice, a meeting in the backroom, and a word everyone in the company is suddenly saying — overhaul. The machine is going to break itself apart and put itself back together, and it's looking for the person who actually knows the building at night.

The backroom, nine in the morning, a table full of managers who have never once closed the store. The regional voice on the speakerphone explains the freight-to-floor overhaul: the whole company restructuring how boxes become shelves.

Stocking 2 gets stripped of its bins and pointed at the trucks. Stocking 1 becomes the bin-and-topstock army. It's a good plan — you can tell, because it sounds like the way you already run the night.
They want me to lead it. The backroom eyes me over the coffee carafe — the closing manager, the one who's actually seen the building break, who's single-handedly closed it a thousand nights.

Same as Lamar, same as the borderlands: when the machine wants something fixed, it sends for the one who knows how it actually runs. I should be flattered. I've watched enough to know what fixing things here costs.

The offer sits on the table. Year two is already running the way year one did — the queues, the blotter regulars, the nights — and now the overhaul wants your head too. What do you do with the year while the machine remakes itself?

Answer the anonymous call that empties the whole building.

nodes.text: I sit the closing crew down before I take another meeting and I tell them the only thing that matters: the overhaul is going to rearrange this building, and nobody on this floor is getting left to ride it alone.

I write down who calls what, who walks the lot, who's got the first thirty seconds of a seizure or a fire or a fight. It's not in the training. It's the second crew I've had to keep alive with nothing but attention.

The call comes in on the store line at 7:52 — a flat, patient voice listing an aisle and a time. You do it by the book, because the book exists for exactly this: the building empties in twelve minutes, the lot fills with the whole neighborhood, police seal the doors.

You walk the listed aisle yourself, the only manager on property, because some things nobody else is going to do. It's nothing — a prank, or a grudge, or a bad night someone wanted to share. The all-clear comes at ten. You reopen to a parking lot of people who waited, because they'd rather be here than home.

A man in the garden lot decides to light a cigarette — leaning against his car, soaked through his jacket with the butane he'd just finished spilling into his own lighter. The flame jumps before the smoke does. He's on fire in the parking lot, screaming, rolling, and there are thirty people watching and exactly one moving.

You don't roll him — a jacket soaked in accelerant doesn't roll out. You strip the jacket off him barehanded, smother his sleeves and his hair, get him down into the gravel, and you stay holding his hand until the medics come. His eyebrows are gone. His face is a raw question. Your wrists are blistered. He's alive.

The building's HR inbox is a blizzard: associate against associate, manager against associate, associate against manager — every one of them using the same two words, discrimination, the word that means everything and nothing at once. You read the docket like a freight list: names, accusations, counter-accusations, three layers deep. And you file your own.

Not because you expect it to move — because the machine has learned that a manager with a file is a manager who's too busy to be trouble. You write it plainly: the closing manager runs a store with no support, and the store calls it policy. You date it, you sign it, and you hand it in with everyone else's.

The regulars come back every week like a weather pattern — the team that sweeps housewares and electronics, the grab-and-run that empties a shelf in eleven seconds. Tonight they've got the service desk in their sights. The blotter is a living thing and it wants the lot. Say 'Enemies' — speak sharp and it lands harder.

We get the carts back, the goods, most of the lot. The regulars scatter into the dark like they always do, and I stand in the doorway with the evening's loss total in my head — not what they took, what the store let them take by staffing a building that size with one manager and no supervisors.

Eleven at night, a dispute in the front row of the lot, and the two men walking toward their cars are both carrying — you saw the first one's hand go to his waist before the words did. The escalation is a live wire. Nobody else is on the lot with a radio. It's you, the dark, and the parking lot drawing. Say 'Enemies' — and hold the line.
I get between the cars before either hand comes out all the way — talk them down, walk them apart, wait until both engines are gone and the lot is only gravel and sodium light.
I stand there with my heart going like a speedbag and I think about how close two strangers came to making this town's news, and how thin the line is that I keep walking down here.

You take the offer. That's the whole sentence — the machine knows how to ask. You'll lead the freight-to-floor overhaul, with Stocking 2 and Stocking 1 both under your hand, and the first metric board goes up in the backroom with your name on it.

The overhaul is surgery on a machine that never stops running. Stocking 2, stripped of the bins that bled their hours, becomes a pure unload team — trucks in, walls down, freight to the floor, fast and clean.

Stocking 1 grows into the bin-and-topstock army that never lets the shelves go hungry. You build the process the way you've built every process: zones, flow, people empowered, numbers as a byproduct of care instead of a whip.
The backroom wall is a whiteboard the size of a bay door. The overhaul won't run itself, and it won't survive a manager who doesn't understand the floor. What do you build first?

choices.text: Rebuild the unload line from the dock to the floor.
Build the bin and topstock army that feeds the shelves.
Push the first impossible metric and see if the machine moves.
Watch the overhaul take hold and see where the numbers land.

nodes.text: You rebuild the unload as a single motion: driver in, dock clear, the line laid out like a rail — case, scan, slot, move on. The old broken system had the freight team buried in bins nobody

could find and clocks that punished the wrong people. You strip it down to the honest job: truck in, wall down, freight to the floor. The crew stops watching the clock and starts watching the trailer.

Stocking 1 becomes the army: bin labels that mean something, topstock run on a ladder of routines, nothing stacked so high the shelves can't breathe. You hand your people the whole map of the building and they start to run it like a body instead of a thousand disconnected parts.

The first monthly number comes back and the machine does what it always does — it wants it faster. The overhaul hits the floor all at once: the dock, the bins, the topstock, the freight wall, the whole rebuild under a clock. This is the day it proves whether it works when leadership actually equips its people. Say 'Enemies' — and run the wall.

The trailer empties, the bins hold, the floor stays fed from open to close. I walk the building at midnight — not closing now, but chosen — and the store is running the way I always believed it could: on the strength of people it finally decided to equip. The board above the backroom says we're climbing. It doesn't say what it'll cost to stay up there.

The email arrives on a Tuesday. The region's quarterly numbers, and your store's name at the top of a list with the number one beside it — in the nation. Number one, out of every area, every region, every store the company runs. The floor that nobody staffed at night, that one closing manager held together with spit and attention, is the best freight operation in the country.

I stand under the board and read it twice. Number one in the nation. We built it — the unload, the bins, the floor, the people. There's a kind of light in the backroom that afternoon, the good kind, the kind you

get for five minutes after a job done right. And I know the machine didn't build it and won't protect it. The machine will want to know how to siphon it — the way it always does with anything that shines.
The shine brings visitors. The machine doesn't reward peak operations by taking care of the people who made them — it sends executives to stand in the light and pretend it was theirs.
The email says a Regional Compliance Manager is coming to spend time with your team. The word is he's being groomed for Area Manager. The word is he has never once read a stocking report in his life.

Richard. Pressed shirt, new badge, a smile that's been practiced in front of a mirror. Regional Compliance Manager, on his way up, and your store is the last stop before his promotion. He holds the stocking report like it's a menu in a language he doesn't speak — the bin labels, the turn times, the freight counts, all of it inert to him. Your job, per the region: teach him to read and execute your team's reports. His job, per him: don't let a single thing expose what he doesn't know.

Todd. Electric to finally see the floor the numbers live on. I want to absorb everything you do — the whole pipeline, soup to nuts. Whatever you think I need most. I'm a fast study, I pick things up quick. And afterwards — anything you need from me, anything at all, my door is going to be open. That's the kind of leader I want to be.

They've sent me the man who'll be my boss someday, and he can't read a bin label. And this is the part that never stops being strange: he needs me — badly — and I know it, and he knows I know it, and neither of us is allowed to say it out loud. So I do what the machine has always done: I make him look good. If he looks good, the region looks good, and the region remembers the name standing next to him.
Richard is sincere and completely useless — the most dangerous combination in corporate America. How do you spend his week?

choices.text: Teach Richard the floor one honest hour at a time.
Let Richard shadow the overnight unload until it scares him.
Survive the compliance visit Richard is leading.

nodes.text: I take him aisle by aisle, bin by bin, slow enough that a child could follow and patient enough not to shame him — because it's not his fault the company handed him a job he was never taught.

By Thursday he can read a turn time out loud without wincing. It's the most useful thing I'll ever do for a boss, and I know it'll be repaid at the going rate of a favor in this industry: nothing, at first.
You put him on the overnight unload, just once, so he can see what the reports actually describe. He lasts four hours. He comes back pale, asking how anyone does this every night — and you can tell
he's already editing that sentence for the version he tells his boss. But something in his eyes stuck. It's the first real data he's ever seen about his own region, and he got it from the floor.

The compliance visit is a circus: Richard leading a walkthrough of the store he now half-knows, the regional director at his shoulder, and your team's whole overhaul under the microscope of people who didn't build it. The visit is the boss today — it wants to see whether the shine holds. Say 'Enemies' — and keep the show on the rails.

Richard stumbles twice, corrects himself both times, and I smooth both stitches in front of the director without missing a beat. The visit passes. The shine holds. Nobody knows how thin the difference was between a promotion and a car wreck — except Richard. He looks at me like he's seen the floor for the first time. I look back like I've seen this movie a dozen times.

The promotion lands six weeks later, announced by email: Regional Compliance Manager Richard, now Area Manager, the region's newest voice — the man whose entire comprehension of the operations he now oversees was installed in one week in your store by a closing manager nobody staffed. There is a delicious hypocrisy in it, and you can taste it for about as long as you let yourself.

His first act as Area Manager is to roll out a process improvement that reads exactly like the words I used in his training — credited to nobody in particular, certainly not to the store that invented them.
I know the going rate of a favor in this industry, and it is what I expected: nothing but the privilege of watching the climber climb. That's the system. I don't hate him for it. I can't afford to.

And now the store itself: the man at the top, the store manager everyone knows by first name before they call the office by its real one — Jay-Dau. And the two store leads in the crossfire of everything that building is. The final contradiction of Pueblo was rolling toward you the whole time, and it has your name on it too.

Jay-Dau is the store manager, and Jay-Dau is also your friend, and the two facts never meet in the same room. Off the clock he's the best company the job ever gave you — beer at the kitchen table, honest talk about the machine, the two of you laughing like the building doesn't own you. On the clock he is pure hell: driven, relentless, and utterly willing to hand you to the machine if his standing costs less than you do. You've seen both versions. You've never seen them apologize to each other.

Off the clock you know I'm your guy, Todd. You know that — man to man, I've got you. On the clock, hey, the clock pays us, you know how it is. The numbers come down, and the numbers don't care whose feelings they land on. Don't take it personal. It's just business. It's always just business.

And under him, the store leads. Amandy — small, precise, furiously energetic, and the most hostile presence in the building, spitting impossible numbers and chaotic demands like they were policy. And Steffie — warm to your face, always in your corner, always offering to take care of it personally — and carving you up in meetings the second the door closes. Two styles, one effect: the floor can't trust either one, and the floor knows it.

Listen, manager. The number is the number. I don't care if it's possible, I care if it's done. You figure out the how — that's what they pay you for, right? And don't come back with excuses. Kitchen table, soapbox, whatever they told you in training. Up here, there's the number, and there's everything that isn't the number. Guess which one I'm writing down.

Hey, Todd — I just want you to know I'm in your corner. Always have been. If anyone's been saying things about you, you come tell me, and we take care of it together. That's what this office is for — we take care of each other. You're doing such a good job with that overhaul. I keep telling everyone. I really do.

The office is a minefield and the friend is upstairs. The paradox of Pueblo's leadership is the last great lesson of the store — Jay-Dau will throw you to save his standing, Amandy's chaos never stops, and Steffie's smile is doing subtraction behind your back. What do you do with the contradiction?

choices.text: Keep the off-the-clock friend and learn the on-the-clock monster.
Survive the clock version with everything he's throwing.
Stand in the path of Amandy's chaos and hold the floor.
Decode Steffie's two faces before they swallow you.
Move on and watch the climbers come and go.

nodes.text: Off the clock, Jay-Dau is real — the honest version of the man the machine owns during the day. I keep the friendship because it's the only warm thing in that office, and I keep the wall because I've watched him hand people to the machine to save his standing. The two of us never talk about it. That's the treaty.

You watch Steffie for a week the way you'd watch weather: the sweet voice in the office, the soft laugh, the way she leans in close to say she's on your side. And then the budget meeting — you hear your own plan come

back at you with her name on it, and the silence in the room tells you it's been her name on half the floor's good work for months. Two faces, one spine. You file her away with the rest of the building's anatomy.

The on-the-clock Jay-Dau arrives with the quarterly pressure at his back: impossible freight numbers, a regional call in his ear, and a willingness to hand you to the machine if the numbers need a body. The paradox is the boss today — friend and monster, one face over the other. Say 'Enemies' — this one knows your name.

The building settles, the numbers hold, and Jay-Dau's version of thanks is a hand on my shoulder that means we're square — until the next quarter. I know exactly what he is, and I keep him anyway, because the other version of him is the only friend this building has ever given me.

Amandy at full chaos is a weather system: the impossible demand, the re-done plan, the names she says about the crew within earshot of the crew. Tonight the chaos has the office and it wants your floor. Say 'Enemies' — then hand the impossible number back done.

I take the impossible number, hold the floor, hand it back done — and she doesn't say thank you, because thank you isn't in the dialect. I've stopped expecting it. The floor knows I took it, and the floor's opinion is the only ledger I'm keeping anymore.

And then the machine does the strangest thing it can do to Amandy: it promotes her. Store Lead to Store Manager, another store, another region's problem — the protective hierarchy stripped away, the sink-or-swim she never had to face. And within three weeks the emails start: 'Todd. I don't know who else to ask. They're eating me alive. You ran that floor. Tell me what to do.'

I answer every email. Every single one — the processes, the crews, the hour-by-hour of how you keep a floor alive when nobody's watching your back. The tyrant who tormented me six months ago is now my most honest student, and I teach

her the way I've taught everyone: because the building doesn't deserve more victims, even when the victim used to be the one holding the whip. She lands the next promotion. She never says thanks. I didn't do it for the thanks.

And meanwhile, underneath the whole show, the store has been keeping its darkest secret in the hours you've never had to work — until now. The overnight operation has a graveyard nobody talks about. Thirteen managers in a single year. You've watched them come and go without learning a single name — because by the time you'd have learned one, they were already gone.

Past midnight the store belongs to a different species. The overnight stocking shift gets its own manager — hired, trained, burned out, and discarded so fast the office stopped printing name badges. In the year of your overhaul, Jay-Dau went through thirteen of them.

You watched from the day shift, assigning each one a number the way you'd log a freight count. One resigned in a month. Two walked out at three in the morning and never came back. Three was let go after a walkie incident nobody will describe. Four through thirteen — the exits blur, but the bodies were real.

I stopped learning their names. That's the part I have to confess — I numbered them like freight, because liking them was a tax I couldn't afford. Thirteen people in one year. Thirteen human beings handed to a machine that was built to eat managers and pretend it was their fault. And I told myself every single time: not me. I know what it does. I'd never take that job.

The graveyard keeps accepting volunteers. Jay-Dau keeps asking. And somewhere under all of it, the third scar is already writing itself on your forehead. What do you do while the overnight machine runs?

nodes.text: You learn them the way you'd learn a disaster's history: One, resignation after a month, the letter polite, the face never seen again. Two, walked out at three AM in the middle of a truck, keys left on the baler, never heard from. Three, let go after a failure to communicate that left two associates crying in the break room.

Four's nerves gave out — he vomited in the receiving office and was gone by sunrise. Five quit on his lunch break, left his walkie on the table beside his half-eaten sandwich. Six lasted three weeks and wrote a letter nobody read. Seven through Twelve — each one hired bright, and each one dimmed so fast you could watch it from the day shift like weather. Thirteen lasted eleven days and told Jay-Dau exactly what the store is. Nobody liked Thirteen. Everybody agreed with him.

I do what a day manager can: I walk the overnight crew as they come through my unload, I write the routines down for them, I make sure the freight wall never lands on their shift without a plan. I can't fix the machine that eats their managers — but I can make sure that on the nights I'm in the building, nobody gets eaten on my watch.

You stand on the overnight floor at three in the morning — empty shelves, freight pallets breathing in the dark, and the machine running its gauntlet: the impossible trailer, the silence, the loneliness of a whole building with no one to help. The meat grinder wants you to feel it. Say 'Enemies' — and listen to how loud the building is when it's empty.

I walk out of that empty building at sunrise shaking the way I've never shaken at close. Nothing attacked me. Nothing happened. That's the grinder — it doesn't need to do anything. It just needs to be the only thing in a hundred thousand feet of dark, asking you to carry it alone, forever. I understand Thirteen now. I understand all of them.

So you take it. That's the fatal step, and it's the quietest one you've ever taken: Jay-Dau asks, the money says yes, the exhaustion says anything, and the part of you that watched thirteen people die in the job says one more time — this one's different, this one is me. It's never different. The Overnight Stocking Manager position is yours, and for two months it will eat you the exact way it ate them.

Two months. The overnight shift puts you in the building eleven hours a night, six nights a week, running the freight-to-floor machine you built for the day crew — alone, in the dark, with no supervisors, no backup, and no end to the trailers.
The commute is a river of empty streets at one in the morning and a wall of sunrise at noon. It is the same job, on the far side of a door you swore you'd never open.

The grind is the truth of the graveyard I spent a year watching: nobody helps you, nobody asks how you are, the store only cares that the trailers empty before the day crew arrives. I run my own unload wall, count my own bins, close my own building, and somewhere in the third week I catch myself talking to the baler. That's when the body starts filing its report.

The pain returns the way it always does — the familiar line of fire across the forehead, drawn in the same place as the first two, third entry on the ledger the body keeps for every store in every state. Shingles Outbreak Number Three, with a vengeance. The body has been shouting for three years. Now it's screaming.

The nerve fire hits during a dead hour on the floor — the same burning belt of pain across the forehead, but harder, hungrier, the third time the body keeps score while the machine watches. Fight through it one pallet at a time, the way you've fought through every other thing. Say 'Enemies' — the body is the boss tonight.

I finish the trailer with one hand on the box and one thought that won't stay down: this is the third time, and each outbreak cost me a piece of the life I left the machine to protect. I stand in the dark and I do the math every clerk does when the body starts to fail: what is this job actually worth, against what it's actually taking?

The call comes a week later, and the machine knows exactly how to ask. A store in St. Augustine, Florida — the region's voice, the words honeyed: the overnight slot, a store in the sunshine, a clean slate, a fresh start.

And with it, the paperwork that has been waiting for you since Lamar: the relocation benefit contract. Corporate will pay for the move. Corporate will also own you — if you walk or they fire you, you owe it back, thousands of dollars, in a state two thousand miles from every person you love.

I read the contract before you bring it home — I know what it is, Todd, I've watched you learn it for three years: the collar. Walk away and we owe them; stay and they own us. But I also see the floor you run and the doctor's note you've been hiding, and I know we can't stay here another month.

So here's what I think: we go — together, on our own money, like always — and we let their contract chase us all the way to Florida if it wants. We leave Pueblo owing them nothing, the way we owed nothing to Lamar, the way we owed nothing to the borderlands. I'd rather be broke in Florida with you than rich in a cage.
The contract glows on the kitchen table, and the third scar burns under your hat. Say what needs to be said before the pen touches the page.

I read it twice. Then I look at the door and I remember every time I've left a machine behind, and I think: the only contract that ever held me was the one I signed with my own two hands.

You walk the building one last time, before the lights come on for the next manager — the backroom board with your name still at the top, the freight wall you taught to breathe, the front end where you told a man he was number six

in line and saved five ahead of him first. The building doesn't say goodbye. Buildings don't have to. You say it for both of you, quietly, in the dark, and you leave the keys on the baler the way you'd leave them for a friend.

It's the final boss of the longest act of your life. Say 'Enemies' and speak sharp — this one has been waiting since Lamar.

I take the whole weight of it — every store, every scar, every manager I watched get eaten — and I hold the line like I've held every line: one breath at a time, until the machine runs out of new things to throw. The contract is still there. It will always be there. But I know what it is now. Knowing is the only armor the machine can't claw back.

The pen goes down. End of Act Four. Todd and Adriana leave Pueblo behind with the third scar burning across his forehead — three stores, three states, three entries on the body's ledger — and the relocation contract folded into a coat pocket like a bar tab the machine intends to collect. Ahead: St. Augustine, Florida, at the end of a two-hour drive in the dark, a store that talks like sunshine and a contract that talks like a leash. He knows what he's walking into. He walks in anyway — because that's what the machine does to good people who keep saying yes. The stage is set for the final, catastrophic crucible.

Jacksonville, at the end of the relocation ledger: two thousand miles of moving boxes and promises, and a house that actually holds your wife's laugh. The first morning off the truck is the brightest this chapter gets — and it knows it.

Adriana unpacks the kitchen with the windows open, drinking the humidity like it's a fountain instead of weather. For one whole evening the machine seems to have let go. The first shift is an hour south in the dark. The drive will teach you the shape of things.
We made it. Two thousand miles of taillights and here we are. Look at that light — this place could be good to us, Todd. It could really, finally be good to us.

I want to believe her so badly it hurts behind the ribs. But my body remembers the other promises the machine made, and the scars it delivered instead. I hold her anyway. Whatever comes next, she's the reason I keep showing up.

The commute is its own country: I-95 south in the dead of night, a standard hour when the world cooperates and a soul-crushing three-hour crawl when it doesn't — accidents, construction, snarls that move like the furniture of hell.

South into the dark before the overnight shift; north into the blinding Florida sunrise after twelve to fourteen hours on the floor. Holding you in place: the relocation contract. Walk away or get fired, and you owe it back — thousands, from two thousand miles out.
The road and the collar, both waiting. Say what needs to be said before the first shift south.

The clawback, page by page: corporate paid for the move, and corporate owns you until the miles repay it. Walk before the term, lose the job, and the debt follows you like a second relocation. A leash wearing a loan officer's smile.

Come home when you can, not when they say you can. I'll be awake. I'll be right here. You didn't survive everything else just to hand them your nights, Todd. Whatever this store is — I'm not afraid of it.

The road ahead: headlights, construction walls, and the long dark between two states of exhaustion. Say 'Enemies' and hold your lane — this one wants to be both the fastest and the slowest hour of your life.
The bridge lights finally thin out and the store glows on the horizon like something that knows my name. The road and I have come to terms: it will always be this hard. So will I.

The first night south, odometer ticking like a debt collector: past the truck stops and the swamp-dark billboards, past exits that smell like rain and diesel. The radio dies somewhere around midnight and the hum of sixty-five takes over.

St. Augustine at last — a megamart rising out of the flat, its parking lot a sea of sodium light, its sign a promise the size of a city block. The building talks like sunshine. The contract in your folder talks like a leash.

The St. Augustine overnight floor under new management: a real crew, a real plan, and a store manager waiting at the dock like a father at a recital. Sriniviii shakes your hand with both of his, and for three whole months he will mean it.

Your freight moves like a river. You hear me? A river. I've watched thirteen overnight managers drown in this building, and I've never once seen the unload run like this. You were worth every mile of the transfer.

The golden period: metrics green, bins breathing, the region calling to check which manager finally fixed the night. The curse of the overnight manager looks broken. You let yourself believe it for a season, because the crew believes it too.

And then there is Ohmar. Not loud, not cruel in public — enormous, calm, watchful. The store lead moves through the building like weather: everyone feels him before they see him. His smile is a courtesy. The whole region runs on his particular kind of heat.
You run the night. I run what the night means to the region. Don't confuse the two, and we'll get along fine. The freight moves like a river, they say. Rivers can be moved.
Three months of sunshine while the meters hold green. Say what needs saying before the vacation — the last bright page this memoir owns.
